1.note: Balak is the king of Moab. See how you translated this in Numbers 22:2.

1.q: וְ⁠הָכֵ֥ן לִ⁠י֙ בָּ⁠זֶ֔ה שִׁבְעָ֥ה & פָרִ֖ים וְ⁠שִׁבְעָ֥ה אֵילִֽים
1.note: The implication is that Balaam wants these bulls and rams sacrificed as burnt offerings on the altars he just asked Balak to build. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [kill seven bulls and seven rams as a sacrifice]

3.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **I will declare to you** before the information about **the word of what he makes me see**. Alternate translation: [I will declare to you the word of what he shows me]

4.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Balaam, not to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Balaam said to God]

5.note: Here, **the mouth of Balaam** represents Balaam’s ability to speak, and putting a word there means that Yahweh told Balaam what to say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh gave Balaam a message to speak]

6.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Balaam, and the pronoun **him** refers to Balak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Balaam returned to Balak]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [and there he saw]
The pronoun **his** refers to Balak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [being stationed beside Balak’s burnt offering]

7.note: The author is using **lifted up his oracle** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam began to speak a prophetic message. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he began to declare his prophecy]

7.q: לְכָ⁠ה֙ אָֽרָ⁠ה לִּ֣⁠י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וּ⁠לְכָ֖⁠ה זֹעֲמָ֥⁠ה יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
7.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Telling me to come and curse Jacob for him and to come and denounce Israel]

7.q: לְכָ⁠ה֙ אָֽרָ⁠ה לִּ֣⁠י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וּ⁠לְכָ֖⁠ה זֹעֲמָ֥⁠ה יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
7.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Come and utterly curse the people of Israel for me!]

The names **Jacob** and **Israel** represent the people who are descended from the man Jacob, who was also named Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Jacob … the people of Israel]

8.note: Balaam is using the question form to emphasize that he cannot curse a people whom God has not cursed. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I will not curse anyone, for God has not cursed]

9.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Balaam is speaking of Israel’s life as a distinct nation as if the people **dwells alone**, living apart from all other peoples. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, a people lives as a nation set apart]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Indeed]

Here, the word translated as **it does not reckon itself** could indicate: (1) what the Israelites think about themselves. Alternate translation: [it does not consider itself] (2) what other people think about the Israelites. Alternate translation: [it is reckoned] or [people do not reckon it]

10.q: מִ֤י מָנָה֙ עֲפַ֣ר יַעֲקֹ֔ב וּ⁠מִסְפָּ֖ר אֶת רֹ֣בַע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
10.note: Balaam is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to count the people of Israel, because they are so numerous. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one can count the dust of Jacob, or number even a fourth of Israel!]

Balaam is speaking of the descendants of Jacob as if they were **the dust of Jacob**, which is too plentiful to count. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Jacob, as numerous as dust]

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [or who has counted a number, the fourth of Israel]

The word translated as **a number** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, which uses the verbal form “has numbered.” Alternate translation: [or who has numbered the fourth of Israel]

Balaam is using this possessive form to mean a fourth part of the people of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a fourth of the people of Israel]

The phrase **the fourth of Israel** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. You may want to follow an alternative reading that some scholars have suggested. Alternate translation: [the dust clouds of Israel]

Balaam is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [May I die the same death that upright people die]

Balaam is using the adjective **upright** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are upright]

The point of this comparison is that just as the upright come to a peaceful and blessed **end**, so Balaam wishes his own end to be. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and may my end be as peaceful and blessed as theirs]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **end**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way I finish my life]

11.note: Balak is using the question form to rebuke Balaam and to express his frustration, not to ask for information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Look what you have done to me!]
The word **to** marks **curse my enemies** as the purpose for which Balak **brought** Balaam. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

Balak is repeating forms of the verb **blessed** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you have completely blessed them]

12.note: The terms **answered and said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

12.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֗א אֵת֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָשִׂ֤ים יְהוָה֙ בְּ⁠פִ֔⁠י אֹת֥⁠וֹ אֶשְׁמֹ֖ר לְ⁠דַבֵּֽר
12.note: Balaam is using the question form to emphasize that he must say only what Yahweh tells him to say. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I must be sure to speak only what Yahweh puts in my mouth!]

The phrase **puts in my mouth** represents what Yahweh tells Balaam to say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh commands me to speak]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Balaam speaking before the information about **it**. Alternate translation: [Shall I not be careful to speak what Yahweh puts in my mouth?]

13.q: תִּרְאֶ֣⁠נּוּ & אֶ֚פֶס קָצֵ֣⁠הוּ תִרְאֶ֔ה וְ⁠כֻלּ֖⁠וֹ לֹ֣א תִרְאֶ֑ה וְ⁠קָבְ⁠נוֹ־לִ֖⁠י
13.note: The pronoun **him** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you will see the people of Israel. Only their edge you will see, and all of them you will not see. And curse them for me]

13.q: אֶ֚פֶס קָצֵ֣⁠הוּ תִרְאֶ֔ה וְ⁠כֻלּ֖⁠וֹ לֹ֣א תִרְאֶ֑ה
13.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **all of him you will not see** before the information about **Only his end you will see**. Alternate translation: [All of him you will not see, and only his end you will see]

14.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Balak, and the pronoun **him** refers to Balaam. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Balak took Balaam]

The author is speaking of the top of the Pisgah as if it were a living thing that could have a **head**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the top of the Pisgah]

The word translated as **Zophim** could be: (1) a proper name. Alternate translation: [to Zophim field] (2) the word for “watchmen.” In this case, the field was used for guarding or watching something. Alternate translation: [to the field of watchmen] or [to Watchmen Field]

16.note: Putting a word **in his mouth** represents Yahweh telling Balaam what to say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and told him what he should say]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh said]

17.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Balaam, and the pronoun **him** refers to Balak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Balaam came to Balak]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [where he was]
The pronouns **him** and **his** refer to Balak. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and behold Balak being stationed beside his burnt offering]

18.note: The author is using **lifted up his oracle** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam began to speak a prophetic message. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he began his prophecy]

19.q: לֹ֣א אִ֥ישׁ אֵל֙ וִֽ⁠יכַזֵּ֔ב וּ⁠בֶן אָדָ֖ם
19.note: Here the masculine terms **man** and **son of a man** have a generic sense that includes any human being, both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [God is not a human being, that he should lie, or a mortal]

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and God is not a son of a man, that he should change his mind]

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Has he said he would do something and then not done it]

19.q: הַ⁠ה֤וּא אָמַר֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יַעֲשֶׂ֔ה וְ⁠דִבֶּ֖ר וְ⁠לֹ֥א יְקִימֶֽ⁠נָּה
19.note: Balaam is using the question form to emphasize that God always does what he says he will do. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [He has said, and he will surely do it; he has spoken, and he will surely fulfill it!]

20.note: Balaam is speaking of receiving a command to bless Israel as if it were an object that he had physically **taken**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, I have received a command to bless]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Balaam’s receiving the command before the information about blessing. Alternate translation: [I have received the command to bless]

The pronoun **he** refers to God, and the pronoun **it** refers to the blessing. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and God has blessed, and I cannot return the blessing]

21.q: לֹֽא־הִבִּ֥יט אָ֨וֶן֙ בְּ⁠יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְ⁠לֹא־רָאָ֥ה עָמָ֖ל בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
21.note: Here, Balaam might mean that: (1) there will not be any of the results that come from **iniquity** and **trouble**. Alternate translation: [He has not looked at the results of iniquity in Jacob, and he has not seen the outcome of trouble in Israel] (2) the Israelites have not done any **iniquity** or **trouble**. Alternate translation: [He has not looked at Jacob doing iniquity, and he has not seen Israel making trouble]

Here, the pronouns **He** and **he** could refer to: (1) any person who observes the Israelites. Alternate translation: [No one has looked at … and no one has seen] (2) God. Alternate translation: [God has not looked at … and he has not seen]

21.q: לֹֽא הִבִּ֥יט אָ֨וֶן֙ בְּ⁠יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְ⁠לֹא רָאָ֥ה עָמָ֖ל בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
21.note: Here, **looked at** and **seen** represent God noticing wrongdoing in order to act against it, so Balaam means that God finds no fault to punish among the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He has found no fault to punish in Jacob, and he has found no wrong to act against in Israel]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [anything wicked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [anything troubling]

The possessive form **his God** describes the relationship between Yahweh and the people of Israel: Yahweh is the God whom they worship and who watches over them. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom they worship]

Here, the word **shout** could refer to: (1) a shout of joy for the king. Alternate translation: [and the shout of joy for a king] (2) a battle-cry uttered by the king, indicating the king’s victory. Alternate translation: [and the battle-cry of a king in victory]

22.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the horns of a wild ox** give it great power, so God gives the people of Israel great strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [giving them strength like the powerful horns of a wild ox]

Here, the pronoun **him** could refer to: (1) God. In this case, it means God is like the ox. Alternate translation: [he is like the horns of a wild ox] (2) the Israelites. In this case, it means the Israelites are like the ox. Alternate translation: [they are like the horns of a wild ox]

23.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [there is certainly no divination of any kind against Israel]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **omen**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [no one can look for signs to predict harm against Jacob]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **divination**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [words spoken by diviners]

The expression **it will be said** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will say to Jacob and to Israel]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [it will be said to Jacob and Israel that God has done amazing things]

The people are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of wonder at what God has done for the people of Israel. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Look at the great things that God has accomplished]

24.note: The point of this comparison is that just as a **lioness** and a **lion** rise up with great power, so the people of Israel rise up in strength against their enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [a people rises up as powerfully as a lioness, and lifts itself up in strength like a lion]

24.q: לֹ֤א יִשְׁכַּב֙ עַד יֹ֣אכַל טֶ֔רֶף וְ⁠דַם חֲלָלִ֖ים יִשְׁתֶּֽה
24.note: Balaam speaks of the people of Israel as if they were a lion that **will not lie down until it eats prey and drinks blood of slain ones**, meaning that Israel will not stop fighting until it has completely defeated its enemies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The people of Israel will not rest until they have completely defeated their enemies]

25.q: גַּם קֹ֖ב לֹ֣א תִקֳּבֶ֑⁠נּוּ גַּם בָּרֵ֖ךְ לֹ֥א תְבָרֲכֶֽ⁠נּוּ
25.note: Balak is repeating forms of the verbs **curse** and **bless** in order to intensify his expression of the ideas that they convey. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [You shall certainly not curse him, and you shall certainly not bless him]

26.note: Balaam **answered and said to Balak** using two speech verbs together, which was a natural way to introduce direct speech in the original language. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

26.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֗א דִּבַּ֤רְתִּי אֵלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר כֹּ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֹת֥⁠וֹ אֶֽעֱשֶֽׂה
26.note: Balaam is using the question form to remind Balak that he had already warned him about this. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I certainly spoke to you, saying, ‘All that Yahweh speaks, it I must do.’]

26.q: לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר כֹּ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֹת֥⁠וֹ אֶֽעֱשֶֽׂה
26.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Did I not speak to you that all that Yahweh speaks, it I must do]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what Balaam must do before the information about who determines it. Alternate translation: [I must do everything that Yahweh speaks]

27.note: If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Even so, please come]

Balak is using the phrase **in the eyes of God** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the judgment of God” or “according to what pleases God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it will please God] or [God will judge it to be right]

28.note: The author is speaking of **the Peor** as if it were a living thing that could have a **head**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the top of the Peor]

Here, **the face of represents** the surface of the wasteland that could be seen from the mountain peak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the surface of the wasteland]
